candidates.name: Horizontal / vertical bar
candidates.editorialExample: Largest data center projects by MW
candidates.caution: Start the value axis at zero for ordinary bars.

textbook.history: William Playfair helped establish the bar chart for comparing economic observations by category rather than following an ordered curve.
textbook.mathematics: The length of each rectangle encodes an amount measured from a common zero, allowing direct magnitude comparison.
textbook.dataRequirements: Use it for one numeric measure across independent named categories, including clearly defined groups and consistent denominators.
textbook.modernInterpretation: Modern reporting uses horizontal bars for megawatt rankings, ASIC shipments by manufacturer, and counts of data-center projects.
textbook.interpretiveRisks: Sorting unordered categories usually helps, while arbitrary category rearrangement or truncated value axes can distort ranking.
textbook.chartComparison: Choose a line for genuine temporal continuity and a dot plot when the value range is narrow relative to a meaningful nonzero baseline.

candidates.name: Pie / donut
candidates.bestFor: A few shares of one complete total
candidates.caution: Shares must sum to the whole; avoid many slices.

textbook.history: William Playfair's early nineteenth-century pie diagram established part-to-whole reasoning; donut variants retain that proportional geometry.
textbook.mathematics: Each sector subtends an angle proportional to its nonnegative share of a single defined total.
textbook.dataRequirements: Require mutually exclusive categories, a common denominator, and only a few proportions that genuinely sum to the whole.
textbook.modernInterpretation: Modern examples include robotics-market revenue shares and technology adoption fractions in a defined hardware fleet.
textbook.interpretiveRisks: Thin slices are difficult to compare and a donut hole adds no new numeric variable by itself.
textbook.chartComparison: Choose sorted bars when exact category ranking matters, or 100-percent stacked bars to compare multiple populations.

textbook.chartComparison: Choose a donut for a few simple fractions or a 100-percent stacked bar for comparisons across several groups.

textbook.history: Filled time-series graphs grew from the same quantitative tradition as Playfair-style line charts, with area emphasizing total magnitude.
textbook.mathematics: At each time point the filled region extends from a fixed baseline to the observed value, so its shape encodes absolute size.
textbook.dataRequirements: Use it for nonnegative, consistently measured sequences when magnitude and cumulative visual weight are more important than precise point comparison.
textbook.modernInterpretation: Modern examples include sustained data-center load, annual energy generation, and the installed capacity of robotics fleets.
textbook.interpretiveRisks: Truncated baselines or unrelated overlapping filled regions can exaggerate amounts and conceal one series behind another.
textbook.chartComparison: Choose a line when slopes and exact changes matter most, and choose stacked area only when components form a meaningful total.

textbook.history: Bubble charts extend scatterplots by introducing a third quantitative dimension, an approach used in multivariate exploratory graphics.
textbook.mathematics: Position encodes two values, while the area of each circle represents a third nonnegative magnitude.
textbook.dataRequirements: Require matched X and Y measurements, a nonnegative size variable, and a defensible area-scaling legend.
textbook.modernInterpretation: Modern comparisons place robotics cost against throughput while using fleet size or shipment volume as bubble area.
textbook.interpretiveRisks: Scaling radius directly to the size value exaggerates large observations because visible area grows with radius squared.
textbook.chartComparison: Choose a scatterplot when the third variable adds little analytical value or a faceted plot when sizes overlap heavily.

textbook.history: Candlestick displays belong to a long Japanese market-charting tradition, later standardized in modern financial analysis for interval quotations.
textbook.mathematics: Each mark encodes four order-statistic-like market observations: open, high, low, and close within one defined interval.
textbook.dataRequirements: Require all four consistently timestamped prices with high at least as large as open and close and low no greater than either.

textbook.interpretiveRisks: Color conventions are not universal, and the display does not reveal intraperiod transaction paths or trading volume by itself.
textbook.chartComparison: Choose a line for a single closing-price series, or a range plot when only interval minima and maxima are available.

candidates.name: Waterfall
candidates.bestFor: How positive and negative changes build a total
candidates.editorialExample: MW added or lost from facility capacity
candidates.caution: Make start, contributions, and end reconcile.

textbook.history: Waterfall charts formalize the accounting bridge between an initial balance, sequential signed changes, and a final total.
textbook.mathematics: Each contribution begins at the previous cumulative level, with increases and decreases algebraically reconciling to the endpoint.
textbook.dataRequirements: Require an initial value, ordered delta contributions, and a final value that can be verified by arithmetic.
textbook.modernInterpretation: Modern data-center reports use them to reconcile capacity added, capacity retired, and available megawatts across a quarter.
textbook.interpretiveRisks: A missing contribution or an inconsistent sign convention breaks the calculation even if the picture looks plausible.
textbook.chartComparison: Choose ordinary bars for independent differences and a time-series line for repeated final balances without explained components.
